title: Andy Burnham's First Weeks as PM: TikToks, Tax Cuts and a Second Downing Street
excerpt: Britain's new prime minister has moved fast with populist spending pledges and a decentralized 'No. 10 North' in Manchester, but questions over funding and factional purges cloud his honeymoon.
body:
• Burnham scrapped VAT on energy bills, capped bus fares at £2, and pledged £340 million to end rough sleeping — all within his first week in office.
  • He established 'No. 10 North' in Manchester's Heron Building, hosting cabinet meetings there four days after taking power as part of his decentralization push.
  • Labour has caught or overtaken Nigel Farage's Reform UK in polls for the first time in over a year, with YouGov showing Burnham viewed as a better PM than any rival leader.
  • Critics say his spending pledges are unfunded, and a purge of Keir Starmer loyalists from cabinet risks deepening Labour's factional divides.

Andy Burnham entered 10 Downing Street on July 20 as Britain's seventh prime minister in a decade, promising to be a "circuit-breaker" for a nation "fed up" with revolving-door leadership. Two weeks later, the 56-year-old former Greater Manchester mayor has delivered a blitz of populist measures, a radical experiment in decentralized governance, and — for the first time in over a year — put Labour ahead of Reform UK in the polls.

Whether any of it is sustainable is already the central question of his premiership.

Spending First, Explaining Later

Burnham's opening moves were deliberately designed for maximum public impact. On his second day, he scrapped the 5% VAT on household energy bills starting October, saving the average household about £45 per year. The government said the £850 million annual cost would be covered by cancelling the previous administration's digital identity card programme. Darren Jones, the former Downing Street chief of staff whom Burnham had fired a day earlier, immediately pointed out that no money had actually been set aside for the ID scheme.

https://x.com/TheNatPulse/status/2084324556014031358

By Wednesday, Burnham announced a cap on single bus fares at £2 from January, funded by redirecting £500 million earmarked for international climate transition projects. The next day brought tax breaks for pubs and small music venues, paid for by raising levies on e-cigarette vendors and online betting shops.

Then came the signature pledge: £340 million over five years to end long-term rough sleeping, with 1,200 homes and intensive support for at least 3,000 people. Officials said the money would come from unused portions of the housing department's budget.

"I know people at home are fed up with politics. I hear you, and I want to be honest with you, we have not been good enough and we need to be better."

— Andy Burnham, outside 10 Downing Street

No. 10 North: Gimmick or Revolution?

Burnham's most audacious move has been establishing what he calls "No. 10 North" — a secondary seat of power in Manchester's Heron Building, facing the gothic spires of the city's Town Hall. On July 24, just four days after forming his government, he hosted part of his cabinet there.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=2H7VSHcYny0

"It is about taking power down and placing it in the hands of people who can use it best," Burnham wrote in The Guardian, calling the office "the nerve centre of a rewired Britain" and "a north pole that balances the south pole" of London.

Sceptics abound. Southern Labour MPs question the reorganization's purpose, noting that deprivation extends well beyond the Northwest — from Northern Ireland to Cornwall. The predominantly right-wing national press has dismissed it as a vanity project. But for Burnham, who spent a decade as Manchester's mayor championing devolution, it is the philosophical core of his pitch.

The Burnham Bounce

For now, the public is responding. A Survation poll found Labour at 26% after Burnham's first week, overtaking Reform UK at 24% — Labour's highest reading with the firm since June 2025 and its first polling lead since May 2025. More In Common showed Labour at 28% versus Reform's 24%. YouGov had the two parties tied at 22%, with Labour up six points since May and more Britons viewing Burnham as a better prime minister than Farage or any other major party leader.

"I won't get carried away," Burnham told reporters, "but I'm pleased to have made a start where hopefully I've connected with people."

Purges and Faction Lines

The goodwill has limits. Burnham's cabinet reshuffle was widely described as a purge of Keir Starmer loyalists. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves and former justice minister David Lammy were removed, replaced exclusively by those who helped Burnham oust Starmer — Ed Miliband, Wes Streeting, and Shabana Mahmood among them.

His appointment of John Healey, Starmer's former defence minister who had resigned in protest at Treasury inflexibility, as chancellor signalled a break from fiscal orthodoxy. Healey had earlier pushed to raise the military budget to 3% of GDP by 2030, a target impossible without significant budget cuts or tax increases. Civil servants have reportedly drawn up plans for a new income levy at 1.8% on earnings above £6,240 to fund social care, though Burnham has said he will wait for an independent review before making any decisions.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 1.6 million people of Indian origin in Britain, Burnham's early moves carry mixed signals. The energy bill cut and bus fare cap offer immediate relief to cost-of-living pressures that have hit immigrant communities hard. But the uncertainty over long-term funding — and the possibility of new taxes — adds a layer of anxiety for small business owners and professionals already navigating post-Brexit economic headwinds.

Burnham's decentralization agenda could benefit cities like Leicester, Birmingham, and Bradford, where large South Asian communities are concentrated. Whether Manchester's gain translates into broader regional investment remains to be seen.

Looking Ahead

Parliament does not return until September, giving Burnham three months before his first Prime Minister's Questions. In the meantime, a social care review by Baroness Casey could reshape his domestic agenda — and his fiscal credibility. Only Theresa May was more popular upon entering Downing Street, back in 2016. Maintaining that standing, Le Monde noted, "could prove difficult over time."
nri_angle: The energy and transport cost cuts offer immediate relief to British Indians, but the uncertainty over future taxes and the decentralization agenda's reach beyond Manchester remain key questions for diaspora communities.
